heading: What will hurt
shape: array of 3 bullet lines per idea
rules: No invented numbers, prices, percentages or timeframes.
Name a real cost or difficulty. Never soften it into a benefit.
Every line must be plausibly true of any small service business, because the pool is shared.

lines.body: The first paying customer takes longer to find than you expect.
Your income is tied to your hours until you find a way to change that.
Nobody is looking for you yet, so the early outreach is all on you.
You will do the work badly the first few times.
Quiet weeks happen and they are hard to plan around.
Chasing payment is part of the job and nobody enjoys it.
You are the sales, the delivery and the admin until you can pay someone.
One difficult customer can absorb a whole week.
There is no salary underneath you while you learn.
Pricing too low at the start is easy to do and hard to undo.
Word of mouth is slow before it is fast.
You cannot take a week off without the income stopping too.
Most of the early enquiries will not turn into work.
You will be judged on your worst job, not your best one.
Nothing here is passive, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something.
You will become extremely familiar with being ignored over email.
The admin arrives uninvited and never leaves.
Everyone wants a quote. Roughly nobody wants to book.
You will explain what you do at least four hundred times.
Your first invoice will take longer to write than the job took to do.
Somebody will ask for a discount before you have even finished the sentence.
The boring parts are not optional, which is a shame, because they are boring.
You will have a week where the phone does not ring once. It is character building.
There is no one to blame, which sounds freeing until something breaks.
Holidays now cost you twice: the trip, and the work you did not do.
Your family will keep asking when you are getting a real job.
The customer who pays least will somehow need the most attention.
You will redo something for free and tell yourself it was good practice.
Spreadsheets. Sorry, but yes, spreadsheets.
Momentum takes months and disappears in about a week if you stop.
The early months are lonely and nobody warns you about that part.
You will feel like you are doing it wrong long after you are doing it right.
Asking strangers to pay you is uncomfortable and it stays uncomfortable for a while.
Nobody hands you a plan. You have to decide what happens next, every week.
Rejection is frequent early on and it does sting.
There is no manager to tell you whether you did enough today.
You will compare yourself to people who started years earlier.
Progress is invisible for a long time before it is obvious.
You have to keep going on the days nothing happens, and most days nothing happens.
It is easy to spend a month preparing instead of asking anyone.
You will need to learn things you did not sign up to learn.
Confidence arrives after the work, not before it, which feels backwards.
Nobody will notice you have started. You have to tell them.
The first no feels personal even when it is not.
There is no clear finish line, so it is hard to know when to rest.
Anything easy to copy gets copied, and this is not hard to copy.
A cheaper competitor can appear at any point and take the price-led customers.
Tools that make this easier for you make it easier for everyone else too.
Demand can move without warning and you find out late.
Whatever channel brings you customers today can change its rules tomorrow.
If a larger operator decides to enter, they will not ask your permission.
Customer expectations keep rising and nobody sends you the memo.
What differentiates you now becomes the baseline within a year or two.
Being early is only an advantage if you keep moving.
Rules and requirements in any trade can change and compliance lands on you.
Attention is the expensive part now, and it gets more expensive.
A single bad public review travels further than ten good private ones.
The moat here is thin. Service is the only thing holding it.
Any advantage built on a tool disappears when the tool gets popular.
Nothing about your position is permanent. It has to be re-earned.
Posting about the work is a second job and it does not pay directly.
Attention is not the same as customers and the gap is wider than it looks.
You have to show up consistently long before anyone is watching.
Building in public means your mistakes are public too.
An audience takes months and does not convert the way people claim.
You can get the marketing right and still have an empty week.
The photogenic version of the job is a small part of the actual job.
Comparison is constant once you start watching others in the same space.
The content only works while you keep making it.
People will engage with your posts and never once buy anything.
Being visible invites opinions you did not ask for.
Referrals dry up if you stop asking, and asking feels awkward every time.
Every platform you build on can quietly stop showing you to people.
Documenting the work eats the hours you needed for the work.
The first hundred posts do almost nothing and you still have to make them.
Cash flow is lumpy and it does not care about your fixed costs.
You cannot grow past your own hours without hiring, and hiring is its own problem.
Concentration risk is real: lose one large customer and the month collapses.
Quoting badly once costs you the margin on the whole job.
Scope creeps unless you write down what is included, and most people do not.
Late payers set your cash flow, not your invoice terms.
Every hour spent on admin is an hour not sold.
You are the single point of failure until the process is written down.
Discounting to win early work sets a price you will fight for years.
Utilisation, not the day rate, decides what you actually earn.
Standards slip the moment you are busy, and busy is when they matter.
Taking on the wrong customer costs more than turning down the right one.
If you do not track where work comes from, you cannot repeat it.
Growth exposes every shortcut you took to get started.
There is no one above you to catch the mistake before the customer does.
Some people will take the quote and go straight to someone cheaper.
You will work a Saturday you did not want to work.
There is always one who argues about the bill after the job is done.
Nobody pays you for the travelling, the waiting, or the phone calls.
If you are sick, nothing gets done and nothing comes in.
The first year you are cheap because you have to be.
People cancel last minute and it is your day that is gone, not theirs.
You will redo a job for free just to keep the peace.
Feast and famine. Some months are mad, some months are nothing.
The paperwork does not do itself and nobody is paying you for it.
There is always someone new undercutting you who does not know their costs.
You have to ask for the money. Every time. Out loud.
One bad job and the whole street hears about it.
You will spend evenings doing the bits you could not fit in the day.
Nobody is coming to help. That is the deal.
The unglamorous truth: most of the first year is finding people, not doing the work.
Three things that catch people out: slow start, unpaid admin, and no safety net.
It does not compound until you have done it consistently for months.
You will want to quit somewhere around the point it starts working.
The skill is learnable. The persistence is the filter.
Nobody tells you how much of this is following up on silence.
The income does not arrive in a straight line and that is hard to live with.
Your time becomes the bottleneck long before your marketing does.
Stopping for two weeks undoes more momentum than you would think.
You will underprice the first ones. Everyone does. It still hurts.
The systems you skip at the start are the ones that break when it gets busy.
Most people quit before the feedback loop finishes one full turn.
Doing the work and selling the work compete for the same hours.
There is no external deadline, so discipline has to come from you.
You cannot outsource the early part, and the early part is the hard part.
It takes longer than anybody tells you. It always has.
You will lose money on a job at some point. Everyone does, once.
Reputation takes years to build and one careless week to dent.
There will be a season with no work. Save for it before it arrives.
The body and the patience both wear down if you never take a break.
Working for yourself means the worry follows you home.
You will be tempted to take work you should have refused.
Nobody pays for the years you spent learning to do it properly.
Trust is slow. There is no shortcut, and people keep looking for one.
The quiet months test you more than the busy ones.
A handshake is not a contract, and you learn that the expensive way.
Keeping records is dull and the day you need them you will be glad.
Pride will make you say yes to a job you have no business taking.
You cannot be the cheapest and the best. Choose early.
Nothing about this is steady until you have made it steady yourself.
You will spend more time chasing people than doing the actual work.
Half the people who say they are interested will disappear without a word.
There is no one to complain to when it goes wrong. It is you.
You will undercharge, resent it, and do it again the following month.
People will expect free advice and call it a quick question.
Nobody is impressed that you started. They want to see you still here next year.
The admin is relentless and it is entirely unpaid.
You will be interrupted constantly and still be expected to deliver.
Boundaries have to be set by you, and enforcing them costs you work.
If you do not ask for the money, you will not get the money.
Being good at it is not enough. Being findable matters just as much.
You will explain your price to someone who was never going to pay it.
The moment it starts working is the moment it gets harder to manage.
Nobody hands you time for this. You take it from something else.
It will take over your evenings before it pays for them.
